messages.content:
Join these diary notes into one flowing paragraph, without the day labels.

Monday. Arohi, five, noticed her Ammamma, Rukmini, lying down in the afternoon, which she never did. Arohi stood in the doorway, quiet, holding her doll.
Tuesday. Ammamma coughed a lot. Arohi brought her a glass of water without being asked and patted her hand. "Ammamma, sad?" "Just tired, kanna."
Friday. Ammamma sat in the garden again. Arohi drew her a picture of a sun with a smiling face and said, "For your cough to go away."

On Monday, five-year-old Arohi noticed her Ammamma, Rukmini, lying down in the afternoon, which she never did. Arohi stood quietly in the doorway, holding her doll. On Tuesday, Ammamma coughed a lot, so Arohi brought her a glass of water without being asked and patted her hand. "Ammamma, sad?" she asked. "Just tired, kanna," her grandmother replied. On Friday, when Ammamma sat in the garden again, Arohi drew her a picture of a smiling sun and said, "For your cough to go away."
Rephrase so it sounds less like an order: Send me the photos from the trip by tonight.
Could you send me the photos from the trip sometime tonight, if you get a chance?
Say this in simpler words: Owing to inclement weather conditions, the outdoor assembly has been postponed until further notice.
The assembly outside has been put off because of bad weather. We will tell you the new date later.

Retell this as one paragraph in the past tense, with no quotation marks.

"Kamal, it's your turn to be the ghost!"
"Wooooo!" Kamal flapped a bedsheet over his head, and all the cousins shrieked and ran across the courtyard.
"Again! Again!"
Kamal laughed so much his tummy hurt. Then he saw Bidisha by the pillar, not running.
"Bidisha, why aren't you playing?"
"It's too loud."
Their Pishi was stringing lights nearby. "Bidisha, would you like to be the ghost's helper? You can hold the torch."
Bidisha thought, then took it. When she shone it on Kamal, everyone screamed with laughter, and Bidisha giggled too.

Kamal was told it was his turn to be the ghost. He flapped a bedsheet over his head and went woooo, and all the cousins shrieked and ran across the courtyard. They begged for more. Kamal laughed until his tummy hurt. Then he saw Bidisha standing by the pillar, not running, and asked why she wasn't playing. She said it was too loud. Their Pishi, who was stringing lights nearby, asked if she would like to be the ghost's helper and hold the torch. Bidisha thought, then took it. When she shone it on Kamal, everyone screamed with laughter, and Bidisha giggled too.
I need a short photo caption from this: We spent a wonderful afternoon at the beach, building sandcastles and chasing the waves with all our cousins.
Sandcastles and waves with all the cousins.

Rewrite these lines in clear modern prose.

The glory of Ikshvaku's line
Made offer of a thousand kine,
And sought to buy at lordly price
A victim for the sacrifice.
To many a distant land he drove,
To many a people, town, and grove,
And holy shades where hermits rest,
Pursuing still his eager quest.
At length on Bhrigu's sacred height
The saint Richika met his sight
Sitting beneath the holy boughs.
His children near him, and his spouse.

The king, the glory of Ikshvaku's line, offered a thousand cows and tried to buy a victim for the sacrifice at a royal price. He travelled to many distant lands, peoples, towns and groves, and to the holy places where hermits rest, still pursuing his eager search. At last, on the sacred height of Bhrigu, he saw the saint Richika sitting under the holy branches, with his children and wife beside him.

Put what people say here into reported speech.

Dolma had been sick with a cough and fever for three days. She was proud of drinking from a big-girl cup, but now she asked for her old baby bottle from the cupboard. She talked in a squeaky baby voice and crawled into Preeti's bed every night. Her aunt laughed, 'Such a big girl, acting like a baby!' Dolma hid her face. Preeti said gently, 'She's poorly. It's fine,' and filled the bottle with warm water. A week later, fever gone, Dolma pushed the bottle away herself. 'That's for babies.'

Dolma had been sick with a cough and fever for three days. She was proud of drinking from a big-girl cup, but now she asked for her old baby bottle from the cupboard. She talked in a squeaky baby voice and crawled into Preeti's bed every night. Her aunt laughed and said that she was such a big girl, acting like a baby. Dolma hid her face. Preeti said gently that Dolma was poorly and that it was fine, and filled the bottle with warm water. A week later, with the fever gone, Dolma pushed the bottle away herself and said that it was for babies.

Report what everyone says without quotation marks.

It rained all morning, so recess at Keerthana's new school in Bengaluru happened inside, in a hot, noisy classroom. Keerthana sat by the window while the others played a clapping game she did not know. When Reena came over, Keerthana said, "In my old school in Coimbatore, nobody ever fought. We all shared everything." Reena nodded. "Even the swing?" Keerthana opened her mouth, then shut it. There had been a swing, and there had been Abinaya, who never let anyone else on it, and that one day Keerthana cried behind the water tank. "Well," she said slowly, "mostly." She still missed the old classroom with the fan that squeaked. But she let Reena teach her the first clap.

It rained all morning, so recess at Keerthana's new school in Bengaluru was inside, in a hot, noisy classroom. Keerthana sat by the window while the others played a clapping game she did not know. When Reena came over, Keerthana said that in her old school in Coimbatore nobody ever fought and they all shared everything. Reena asked whether that included the swing. Keerthana opened her mouth, then shut it. There had been a swing, and there had been Abinaya, who never let anyone else on it, and that one day Keerthana cried behind the water tank. Slowly she said that it was mostly true. She still missed the old classroom with the fan that squeaked, but she let Reena teach her the first clap.

Make this fit a toddler's picture book, with short sentences and simple words.

Two-year-old Uday was riding on his mother Harsha's hip down the village lane when he saw the tractor parked by the well. He gasped and pointed. "Face! Face!" Two round headlights, a wide grille like a grin. Uday kicked his legs, laughed, then waved at it. "Hi!" Harsha laughed too. "Yes, it's smiling at you." Uday wriggled to be put down so he could pat its nose.

Uday rode on his mother's hip down the village lane. He saw a tractor by the well. He gasped and pointed. "Face! Face!" The tractor had two round lights and a wide front like a big grin. Uday kicked his legs and laughed. He waved and said, "Hi!" Harsha laughed too. "Yes, it is smiling at you," she said. Uday wriggled to be put down. He wanted to pat the tractor's nose.
Hide the doer by using the passive voice: Someone has locked the gate.
The gate has been locked.

Prose, not verse, please, and keep the events in the same order.

And Kusik's son approved his speech,
And moving to the sandy beach,
Placed in the boat the hermit band,
And reached the river's further strand.
On the north bank their feet they set,
And greeted all the saints they met.
On Ganga's shore they lighted down,
And saw Visala's lovely town.

Kusik's son approved of his words. He went to the sandy beach, put the band of hermits into the boat, and reached the far shore of the river. They stepped onto the north bank and greeted all the saints they met. They landed on the shore of the Ganga and saw the lovely town of Visala.
Use one word in place of the long phrase: She is a person who teaches music.
She is a music teacher.
Agenda items should be short, so trim this: Discussion about the problems with the printer in the office.
Problems with the office printer

Can you condense this to under 60 words?

My sister Kavitha had a science fair coming up, and I watched her spend Saturday morning on the floor of our room with a notebook. She wrote question after question. I read some upside down: "Why does ice float? Do plants like light? Can a spider smell?" She had ten. Then she started crossing them out. I don't know what she was thinking, but she kept looking around the room, at the window, at the cupboard, at Amma's plant pots on the balcony. By lunch she had only one left: "Do plants lean towards light?" She went to Amma and asked for two small pots. Our neighbour Naveen uncle gave her some bean seeds. By evening the pots were ready.

My sister Kavitha spent Saturday morning in our room writing ten science fair questions in a notebook. She crossed out all but one: "Do plants lean towards light?" She asked Amma for two small pots, and our neighbour Naveen uncle gave her some bean seeds. By evening the pots were ready.
Change this from first person to third person, about Aarav: I woke up late, and I missed my bus, so I walked to school with my umbrella.
Aarav woke up late and missed his bus, so he walked to school with his umbrella.
Combine into one sentence with "because": I could not call you. My phone had no battery.
I could not call you because my phone had no battery.

Rewrite this so a child could understand it, in short sentences.

Usually, when the app goes down, our lines explode and we have nothing to tell anyone. This time Leela was named communications owner.
Usually, when the app stops working, everyone contacts us at once, and we have nothing to tell them. This time Leela was chosen to give the news.
Make this more courteous: I want a refund for this bag. It's torn.
Excuse me, I would like a refund for this bag, please. It is torn.
Rewrite so it is polite: I want some water.
May I please have some water?

Rewrite in the third person (she) for Ms Roy.

I keep a diary, and I write in it every night.
Ms Roy keeps a diary, and she writes in it every night.
